1.text:
The verse opens with an instruction, not a statement. The first word the translation gives you is *Say* — and that single word decides everything about how the rest should be read. This is not a conclusion the Prophet ﷺ arrived at and is now defending. He is told to announce it. The message arrives from outside the argument.

The occasion explains why it needed announcing. Ubayy ibn Kaʿb relates that the idolaters came to the Prophet ﷺ and said: *"O Muhammad, tell us the lineage of your Lord."* Imām Aḥmad records this, and at-Tirmidhī and Ibn Jarīr carry it with an addition. Some narrations put the same question to the Jews of Madīnah rather than the pagans of Makkah, and one report has them asking whether Allah was made of gold or silver. Because of these conflicting reports the classical scholars disagreed about whether the sūrah is Makkan or Madanī — Ibn Masʿūd, al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī, ʿAṭāʾ, ʿIkrimah and Jābir held it Makkan; Qatādah and aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk held it Madanī; two reports from Ibn ʿAbbās go in opposite directions. The question behind all of them is the same, and it is the question the sūrah answers: *where does your God come from?*

Tanwīr al-Miqbās preserves the sharpest version of the question, on the authority of **Ibn ʿAbbās**: *the people of Quraysh asked the Prophet ﷺ, "O Muhammad! Describe for us your Lord; is He made of gold or silver?" And so Allah revealed this sūrah to describe His attributes and traits.*

Is He made of gold or silver. That is not a theological question. It is a request for a material description — what substance, what shape, what is He out of. And the sūrah's answer refuses the form of the question entirely. It gives no substance, no shape, no genealogy. It gives a Name and a denial.

Ibn Kathīr records the grading of the main report and keeps the disagreement visible: **Ibn Abī Ḥātim** also recorded it, and **at-Tirmidhī** mentioned it as a mursal narration, then said, *"And this is the most correct."*

What he is told to say is deliberately short. *He is Allah.* The Name comes before any description, because the sentence is about who God is rather than what God does. Al-Jalālayn notes the grammar: *Allāh* is the predicate of *He is*, and *One* either substitutes for it or serves as a second predicate — so the sentence states an identity and then defines it.

That definition is *One — and Indivisible*, and the single Arabic word *aḥad* carries both halves. It denies a second: there is nothing alongside Him. And it denies parts: He is not assembled, so nothing can be added to Him, subtracted from Him, or shared out between Him and another. Al-Mukhtaṣar puts it as bluntly as it can be put — He is alone in being a deity; there is no deity except Him.


**What the sūrah became.**

Ibn Kathīr follows the occasion with two reports about how the sūrah was actually used, and both turn on one man's attachment to it.

Al-Bukhārī reported from **ʿAmrah bint ʿAbd ar-Raḥmān**, who used to stay in the apartment of **ʿĀʾishah**, the wife of the Prophet ﷺ, that ʿĀʾishah said: *The Prophet ﷺ sent a man as the commander of a war expedition, and he used to lead his companions in prayer with recitation of the Qurʾān, and he would complete his recitation with "Say: He is Allah, One." So when they returned they mentioned that to the Prophet ﷺ, and he said, "Ask him why he does that." So they asked him, and he said, "Because it is the description of ar-Raḥmān, and I love to recite it." So the Prophet ﷺ said, "Inform him that Allah the Most High loves him."*

Muslim and an-Nasāʾī recorded it too.

Al-Bukhārī records a second, in his Book of Ṣalāh, from **Anas**: *A man from the Anṣār used to lead the people in prayer in the Masjid of Qubāʾ. Whenever he began a sūrah in the recitation of the prayer that he was leading them, he would start by reciting "Say: He is Allah, One" until he completed the entire sūrah. Then he would recite another sūrah along with it. And he used to do this in every rakʿah.*

His companions objected that one sūrah should be enough. What is worth holding is the reason neither man gave — not that it was required, but that he loved it. *It is the description of ar-Raḥmān.*

The sūrah was revealed to answer a demand for a lineage. What it produced instead was the shortest statement of tawḥīd in the Qurʾān, and two men who would not lead a prayer without it.

2.text:
Verse one said *who* He is. Verse two says what that means for everyone else: *Allah — the Sustainer, needed by all.*

The word translated here is *aṣ-Ṣamad*, and it is the one word in the sūrah that the classical commentators found hardest to pin to a single English equivalent — which is why the translation gives it a gloss in brackets. Maʿārif-ul-Qurʾān records that the word carries several literal senses, and that exegetes accordingly assigned it different meanings; aṭ-Ṭabarānī, in his *Kitāb as-Sunnah*, gathered the interpretations and concluded that they are all sound and comprehensive rather than competing. The variety is the point: the word is doing more work than any one rendering can hold.

The sense the translation settles on is the one al-Jalālayn gives most directly — *aṣ-Ṣamad* is the One who is always sought at times of need. Tanwīr al-Miqbās lists the other readings that gathered around it: the Master whose glory is at its peak, to whom all created beings are in need; the One who neither eats nor drinks; the One who has no interior; the Everlasting; the Sufficient; the One who has no entrance through which anything might reach Him. Read together these are not six definitions but one fact approached from six directions: nothing reaches Him, and everything needs Him.

That is the hinge of the sūrah. Verse one removed rivals. Verse two removes independence — not His, but ours. Al-Mukhtaṣar states it in two movements: to Him belongs all sovereignty and every perfect quality, and He is the One to whom all creation turns. Ibn Kathīr, drawing on the same narration from Ubayy ibn Kaʿb, ties it back to what follows: *aṣ-Ṣamad* is the One who neither begets nor is begotten, because whatever is born dies, and whatever dies leaves an inheritance — and Allah neither dies nor leaves one.

So the bracketed phrase in your translation is not a hedge. *Needed by all* is the whole claim.

3.text:
Now the sūrah turns and answers the question it was revealed for. *He has never had offspring, nor was He born.* Two denials, in both directions, and between them the whole of the question that opened the sūrah is closed.

Maʿārif-ul-Qurʾān makes the target explicit: this verse responds to those who asked about Allah's ancestry. The reasoning it gives is not a claim about biology but about category — there is no analogy between the Creator and what He creates. Creation comes into being through procreation; a thing that is begotten is a thing that began. Allah has no children and is no one's child, because begetting and being begotten belong to the order of things that start and end.

Al-Jalālayn compresses the same point into two clauses, and they are worth keeping apart because they deny different things. *He neither begot* — because no likeness of Him can exist, and offspring implies likeness. *Nor was begotten* — because createdness is excluded in His case altogether. The first denial protects His uniqueness; the second protects His eternity.

Ibn Kathīr carries the argument one step further, through the narration of Ubayy ibn Kaʿb. Nothing is born except that it will die, and nothing dies except that it leaves an inheritance behind. Inheritance presupposes an heir, and an heir presupposes a line. Allah does not die and leaves no inheritance, so the chain the idolaters were asking Him to join has no place for Him in it. Tanwīr al-Miqbās puts the same idea in the language of dominion: He has no son who would inherit His rule, and He was not begotten, so He did not receive His rule from anyone.

The translation's phrase *never had* is doing quiet work here. It is not that He had none and then ceased; the tense rules out the possibility itself. Al-Mukhtaṣar states the conclusion flatly — no offspring, and no parent.

A question about lineage assumed a family. The answer is that the question does not apply.

4.text:
The sūrah ends where it began, by removing comparison altogether: *And there is none comparable to Him.*

The word behind *comparable* is *kufuʾan*, and Maʿārif-ul-Qurʾān unpacks it as an example, a similar thing, one equal in rank and position. That triple matters, because it closes three different doors at once. Not merely that nothing looks like Him — nothing *ranks* with Him either. The verse therefore denies resemblance in His attributes, in His acts and in His powers, and it denies it across all of time: no one in the universe is His equal, none ever was, and none ever can be. Ibn Kathīr states it in the plainest available terms — none similar to Him, none equal to Him, nothing at all like Him.

Tanwīr al-Miqbās adds the political sense the word also carried for its first hearers: He has no opposite, no peer, no equal, and no co-ruler who might compete with Him over dominion and sovereignty. For an audience surrounded by pantheons whose gods disputed and divided the world, that was the sharpest edge of the sentence.

Al-Jalālayn notices something in the Arabic worth keeping, because it explains why the verse reads the way it does. The phrase *to Him* belongs in sense to *comparable*, yet it is placed before it, since it is what the negation is aimed at. And *anyone* — the subject of *there is* — is placed after the predicate *comparable* in order to preserve the end-rhyme the sūrah has been keeping. The word order is not loose; it is carrying the emphasis and the sound at the same time.

Read the four verses back as one movement. Verse one: there is no second. Verse two: nothing is independent of Him. Verse three: He stands outside the order of birth and death. Verse four: so there is nothing to measure Him against. The sūrah was asked for a genealogy and gave, instead, the reason a genealogy is the wrong kind of answer.

This is why the Prophet ﷺ called it a third of the Qurʾān — reported by al-Bukhārī and Muslim — and why it has been treated as the essence of the Book: everything the Qurʾān says about who Allah is, this sūrah says in four lines.
